input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_title: Evidence retrieval, ranking, and injection protocol
input.section_summary: Detail the retrieval sources and indexing, query formulation, ranking/scoring of candidate evidence, selection thresholds, and the protocol for injecting ranked evidence into section prompts.

output:
We design the evidence retrieval, ranking, and injection protocol to produce section-level outputs that are explicitly grounded in verifiable sources and that integrate with the JSON-constrained generation and downstream LaTeX assembly. The protocol is organized into five conceptual components: candidate sources and indexing, query formulation, ranking and selection, evidence injection into prompts and JSON outputs, and iterative validation with fallback actions. Below we describe each component and the interactions that enforce conservative, provenance-rich generation.

Candidate sources and indexing
- The protocol treats heterogeneous text sources as queryable corpora. Typical corpora for our workflow include internal author notes, curated PDFs and their extracted full text, and any structured bibliographic records available for the target domain. Each source is represented in the index by (at minimum) full-text tokens and a small set of metadata fields (title, authors, year, document identifier, and page or section offsets).
- Indexing produces two complementary retrieval artifacts: a lexical index for fast sparse retrieval and a lightweight vector index for semantic lookup. Both indices store stable provenance pointers that map retrieved spans back to the original document and location. These provenance pointers are carried forward into the JSON output for every cited evidence item.

Query formulation
- Queries are constructed at section granularity and are conditioned on the section graph context. A section’s retrieval query is seeded from the section title and the section-level goal (as encoded in the document graph), augmented with salient facts or constraints extracted from already-generated prerequisite nodes (leaf-first scheduling supplies these when available).
- The protocol favors structured query templates that separate rhetorical intent (e.g., ``motivate problem'', ``describe prior work'', ``report metric X'') from keyword expansion. The templates are filled with phrases and key terms derived from the target section and from any user-supplied prompts, producing both short keyword queries for sparse retrieval and longer natural-language queries for semantic retrieval.

Ranking and selection
- Retrieved candidate spans are re-ranked by a multi-criteria scorer that combines lexical match, semantic similarity, provenance quality (e.g., presence of a clear bibliographic identifier), and minimal redundancy with higher-ranked items. Ranking is deterministic given the same scorer configuration and inputs to aid reproducibility.
- Selection applies conservative acceptance rules: evidence items must meet provenance completeness (document id and span location present) and a minimum rank quality threshold before being considered eligible for injection. The protocol records the full ranked list and the selection decision for auditability; chosen items are attached to the JSON section under a required evidence field.

Evidence injection into prompts and JSON outputs
- Injected evidence is presented to the generator in two linked forms. First, the prompt-level injection places short, clearly delimited evidence anchors near the top of the generation prompt; each anchor contains a human-readable excerpt (a short span), its provenance pointer, and an explicit instructive tag (e.g., ``use this evidence as support for Claim X''). Second, the JSON output schema exposes an evidence array where each element includes: the selected excerpt text, provenance metadata (document id, page/offset), a machine-checkable citation key, and an annotation slot for the generator to indicate which claims or sentences the evidence supports.
- Prompts explicitly require the model to (a) prefer phrasing that cites the provided evidence anchors whenever making factual assertions that derive from them, and (b) avoid introducing new factual claims that lack attached evidence entries in the JSON evidence array. The generator is instructed to populate the JSON evidence array as part of generation rather than retrospectively.

Iterative validation and fallback actions
- After a section candidate is produced, a validation pass checks the JSON for structural compliance (required fields present), citation coverage (every nontrivial assertion marked as factual must reference one or more evidence items), and basic contradiction heuristics with prerequisite sections. Failures trigger a deterministic fallback sequence: (1) local re-generation constrained to the existing selected evidence; (2) targeted re-retrieval with an amended query emphasizing unsupported claims; or (3) flagging for human review if automated recovery is unsuccessful. All validation outcomes and fallback steps are logged.
- The protocol also supports an explicit ``evidence-conservative mode'' in which the generator is prohibited from asserting factual claims that cannot be linked to at least one selected evidence item; in this mode, unsupported content must be expressed as speculative language or omitted.

Auditability and machine-checkable provenance
- Throughout retrieval, ranking, selection, and injection, the protocol maintains provenance as first-class data: every injected excerpt includes the pointer to the source document and its location, and the section JSON records which sentence-level claims the evidence supports. This provenance enables automatic checks during assembly into LaTeX + refs.bib and simplifies post-hoc adjudication of unsupported assertions.
- The protocol emits two machine-readable artifacts per section: (1) the validated JSON section with evidence array and provenance pointers, and (2) a retrieval report that contains the original ranked candidates, scoring diagnostics, and any applied selection thresholds. These artifacts are stored alongside the generated manuscript to enable reproducible audits and targeted human edits.

Practical notes and integration points
- The retrieval and ranking components are configured as modular services so that different sparse or dense retrievers, or different re-rankers, can be swapped with minimal disruption to the injection and validation logic. Implementation-specific parameters (e.g., size of candidate pools, score cutoffs) are treated as tunable hyperparameters and are selected in the experimental protocol (Section 4).
- The design emphasizes conservative defaults: prefer higher provenance quality and explicit citation links over maximizing evidence quantity; prefer repeating the provenance pointer in the JSON for every claim supported by the same source rather than assuming implicit coverage across a section.

Limitations and scope statement
- The protocol described above is a design for evidence-aware section generation; implementation choices (indexing technology, exact scoring formulas, and numerical thresholds) are implementation details that must be reported with any empirical evaluation. Because the present manuscript focuses on the protocol and its integration with graph-aware scheduling, empirical parameter tuning and ablation analyses appear in the Experiments and Results sections (Section 4 and Section 5).
